title: Spontaneous regression of tumor in a girl with optic pathway glioma with diencephalic syndrome
content: To the editor:A 6‐month‐old girl presented with poor appetite but no vomiting or other gastrointestinal symptom. There was no significant increase in her body weight for 2 months. Her birth weight was 3.4 kg. She also had horizontal nystagmus 2 days before her initial visit. Physical examination showed that the patient had bilateral horizontal nystagmus and left esotropia. Poor visual acuity was found on the left side, but good acuity on the right. No café‐au‐lait macule was found on her body. Visual activity examination and flash visual evoked potential (FVEP) by the ophthalmology department failed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a 42 mm × 37 mm × 36 mm enhanced and lobulated lesion with a large cystic component at the bottom located in the sellar region with a clear boundary with surrounding tissues (Figure 1A, B). The optic chiasm and optic nerve nearby could not be recognized. Optic pathway glioma (OPG) and diencephalic syndrome (DS) were diagnosed according to the history and the characteristics of the MRI. No family history of tumor including neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF‐1) was found. Considering the low age and low body weight of the patient, her parents refused surgical treatment. Close follow up (3 months) was suggested.FIGURE 1Magnetic resonance imaging of a girl with optic pathway glioma and diencephalic syndrome. (A) Sagittal and (B) axial enhanced MRI images of the patient at her age of 6 months and 20 days. (C) Sagittal and (D) axial MRI images of the patient at her age of 1 year and 11 months old. Tumor size shrunk obviously from 42 mm × 37 mm × 36 mm to 38 mm × 35 mm × 23 mm. A newly generated cystic component that seemed like an arachnoid cyst (18 mm × 35 mm × 26 mm) formed at the left temporal pole.One month later, horizontal nystagmus of the patient disappeared. However, her body weight declined continuously and came to the lowest point of 4.5 kg at the age of 1‐year‐old. The patient's appetite and food intake increased gradually after the age of 1 year. The MRI of the patient at 1 year and 11 months of age showed the size of the tumor reduced to 38 mm × 35 mm × 23 mm (Figure 1C, D). A newly generated cystic component that seemed like an arachnoid cyst formed at the left temporal pole.The girl grew to 10 kg at the age of 2 years and 2 months. She seemed to recover from DS. Her parent did not find a remarkable decrease in her vision and horizontal nystagmus did not appear again. Visual activity examination and flash visual evoked potential showed she had a moderate retardation of her left eye and a normal signal of the right eye.Optic pathway gliomas are special gliomas originating in the visual pathway, usually found in children under 10 years of age. The biological behaviors of OPGs are unstable. Some can remain stable for a long time but some grow or spread rapidly, and several even shrink or disappear naturally. 1 , 2 , 3 Optic pathway gliomas also lead to various endocrine changes, including DS. 4 Diencephalic syndrome can lead to difficulty in gain weight in pediatric patients, usually secondary to neoplastic lesions nearby hypothalamus, was closely related to the OPGs. 5 Some studies have shown that OPG patients with DS have a poor prognosis. Gropman et al. 6 found that the average survival time of untreated OPGs patients with DS was usually less than 1 year. 6 Rakotonjanahary et al. 7 reported that girls with OPG and DS had a poor prognosis. In this case, without any treatment, the tumor size reduced and DS improved.Natural regression of tumors including central nerve system tumors has been reported. Brzowski et al. 8 first reported a 2‐year‐old boy with NF‐1 who developed a natural regression of optic glioma. Natural regression was mostly observed in patients with NF‐1. 3 However, Parsa et al. 9 reported that 13 children with optic glioma had natural regression, nine of whom did not have NF‐1. The mechanism of natural regression of OPG has not been clearly studied. Some researchers thought that it was mostly due to the shrinking of cystic components. However, some studies had shown tissue regression of astrocytoma located in several positions. 10 Some believed reduced proliferation could be secondary to enhanced immunocompetence and immune recognition of tumors. 9 Treatment for OPG patients with DS is still controversial. Parsa et al. 11 , 12 thought that OPGs should be categorized as hamartomas rather than neoplasms; therefore they should not be treated, even if there is an evidence of clinical or radiographic progression. However, some believed this kind of tumor still belongs to the neoplasm. 13 Thiagalingam et al. 14 showed that the reduction of tumor size was not always positively correlated with the patients’ visual function; the vision of some OPG patients with natural regression could remain stable or even deteriorate. During the follow up of this case, we found the original nystagmus of the patient disappeared and the emaciation caused by DS gradually improved, but the left eye vision did not improve. We thought that body weight may reflect the progression of OPG patients with DS better than visual activity. As far as we are aware, this is the first case in which spontaneous regression occurred in an OPG patient accompanied by DS. Even though patients with DS always showed a worse outcome, for children with recent weight gain, close follow up may be a choice.CONSENT FOR PUBLICATIONWritten informed consent was obtained from the parents.CONFLICT OF INTERESTThe authors declare no competing interest.

diagnosis.diagnosis_raw: Optic pathway glioma (OPG) and diencephalic syndrome (DS) were diagnosed according to the history and the characteristics of the MRI.
diagnosis.disease_name: optic pathway glioma with diencephalic syndrome
diagnosis.severity_description: Large sellar-region lesion with diencephalic syndrome (failure to gain weight/emaciation)
diagnosis.prognosis_given: Average survival time of untreated OPGs patients with DS was usually less than 1 year (cited literature).
diagnosis.quality_of_life_impact: Poor appetite; no significant weight gain for 2 months; progressive weight loss/emaciation to 4.5 kg by age 1; visual impairment left eye; nystagmus; left esotropia.
diagnosis.disease_duration_before_healing: From ~6 months old to at least 1 year 11 months old (tumor shrinkage observed on follow-up MRI).
diagnosis.primary_site: Sellar region/optic chiasm-optic pathway region (optic chiasm and optic nerve not recognized on MRI)

treatment.treatments_raw: Parents refused surgical treatment; close follow up suggested.
treatment.treatment_stopped_reason: Parents refused surgery due to low age and low body weight.

remission_outcome.time_to_remission_raw: Tumor shrinkage observed on MRI at age 1 year 11 months (from 6 months 20 days baseline).
remission_outcome.verification_detail: MRI tumor size decreased from 42×37×36 mm (age 6 months 20 days) to 38×35×23 mm (age 1 year 11 months). Clinical DS improved with weight gain to 10 kg by age 2 years 2 months; nystagmus resolved after 1 month and did not recur.
remission_outcome.tumor_response: Tumor size shrunk obviously on follow-up MRI; DS improved clinically.
remission_outcome.tumor_size_change: 42×37×36 mm → 38×35×23 mm; new cystic component at left temporal pole described as arachnoid-cyst–like (18×35×26 mm).
remission_outcome.follow_up_duration_raw: Follow-up described through age 2 years 2 months (baseline at 6 months 20 days; MRI at 1 year 11 months).

agency_examples: Parents refused surgical treatment due to low age/low body weight and chose close follow-up.
turner_factors.agency_details: Decision to refuse surgery and pursue close follow up.

validation.statistical_improbability_notes: OPG with diencephalic syndrome is described (cited literature) as having poor prognosis when untreated; nevertheless tumor size decreased and DS improved without treatment.
validation.extraction_notes: No histology/biopsy confirmation; remission is partial (size reduction) with clinical improvement of DS; follow-up duration not fully specified beyond age 2y2m.

analysis.case_summary: A 6-month-old girl diagnosed by MRI with a large sellar-region optic pathway glioma and diencephalic syndrome had no surgery or other treatment (parents refused). Over follow-up, her nystagmus resolved, weight recovered, and MRI at 1 year 11 months showed tumor shrinkage from 42×37×36 mm to 38×35×23 mm, consistent with spontaneous partial regression.
key_healing_factors: No conventional treatment; close follow-up only
Spontaneous tumor size reduction on serial MRI
Clinical improvement of diencephalic syndrome with later weight gain
unique_features: OPG accompanied by diencephalic syndrome with spontaneous regression reported as first such case by authors
New arachnoid-cyst–like cystic component noted on follow-up MRI
Neurologic/visual symptoms improved for nystagmus but persistent left-eye visual deficit
analysis.analysis_notes: Narrative contains no psycho-spiritual factors; the only Turner-related element is parental agency/refusal of surgery. Regression is documented radiographically but not complete; no long-term durability beyond early childhood is provided.
